label: Measure Concentration and Almost Spherical Sections
notes: This chapter, spanning printed pages 329 through 354, develops the high-dimensional phenomenon that smooth functions on the sphere barely move away from a single value. We trace that fact from isoperimetry through Lipschitz concentration and finish with Dvoretzky's theorem on almost spherical sections of convex bodies.

label: High-Dimensional Surprise
notes: Intuition trained in two or three dimensions fails badly on the sphere of large dimension. Almost all of the surface measure sits within a thin band around any equator, and the mass spreads ever closer to it as the dimension grows. This counterintuitive packing of measure is the engine of the chapter.

label: The Sphere and Its Measure
notes: We fix the unit sphere with its rotation-invariant probability measure and the geodesic metric. Working with a normalized measure lets us speak of the probability that a random point lands in a region, which is the natural language for the concentration estimates that follow throughout the chapter.

label: Levy Isoperimetric Inequality
notes: The isoperimetric inequality on the sphere says that among all sets of a given measure, spherical caps have the smallest neighborhood enlargement. Comparing any half-sphere to its t-enlargement gives the sharp bound that drives concentration: the complement of a halved set shrinks exponentially in the enlargement radius.

label: The Equatorial Band Carries the Mass
notes: Taking the set to be a closed hemisphere, its t-neighborhood is a band around the equator. Isoperimetry forces the measure outside that band below exp of minus t squared n over two. So a band of fixed angular width already captures essentially all measure once the dimension is large.

label: Lipschitz Functions Concentrate
notes: A function that does not stretch distances cannot vary much where almost all the measure lives. Applying the band estimate to the sublevel and superlevel sets of a one-Lipschitz function shows it stays within t of its median except on a set of measure at most twice exp of minus t squared n over two.

label: Median versus Mean
notes: Because the deviation tails are exponentially small, the median and the expectation of a Lipschitz function differ by only a constant over the square root of the dimension. This lets us state concentration around either centering value, a convenience used repeatedly when estimating averages of random projections.

label: Gaussian Concentration
notes: The same phenomenon appears for the standard Gaussian measure in high dimension, where a one-Lipschitz function concentrates around its mean with a clean dimension-free sub-Gaussian tail. Gaussian concentration is often easier to apply because the coordinates are independent and the norm concentrates near the square root of n.

label: Almost Spherical Sections
notes: A central section of a symmetric convex body is almost spherical when its norm is squeezed between two close multiples of the Euclidean norm. The eccentricity epsilon measures how round the section is. The goal is to guarantee such a section of large dimension inside an arbitrary body.

label: Dvoretzky's Theorem
notes: Dvoretzky's theorem states that every n-dimensional symmetric convex body has a central section of dimension proportional to log n over epsilon squared that is epsilon-close to a Euclidean ball. The dimension of the round slice grows without bound as the ambient dimension increases, no matter how distorted the body is.

label: Proof Strategy via Nets
notes: The proof picks a random subspace and shows the norm is nearly constant on its unit sphere. Concentration controls the norm at each point, an epsilon-net discretizes the sphere of the subspace, and a union bound over the net keeps the failure probability small while the net size stays exponential in the subspace dimension.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Concentration of measure converts high dimension from an obstacle into structure: Lipschitz functions flatten, mass hugs equatorial bands, and random low-dimensional sections of convex bodies become almost round. These ideas reappear across embeddings, random projections, and the probabilistic method throughout discrete geometry.
